summary:
ORBITAL (Know Your Signal) is an offline-first astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed for long-duration spaceflight scenarios. It enables crew members to record 14 health indicators, review personal trends, identify potentially concerning changes through rule-based alerts, and prepare a seven-day health summary for flight-surgeon handoff.

The application features an interactive eight-system body map, health measurement tracking, wellbeing check-ins, an exercise and countermeasure coach, offline medical information responses, and a 180-day synthetic mission simulator. It supports five mission contexts: ISS/low Earth orbit, Orion transit, lunar base, Mars transit, and Mars surface.

Built as a single standalone HTML application using HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and SVG, ORBITAL requires no installation, backend, account, API, or continuous internet connection. Its purpose is to demonstrate how locally available health records, explainable alerts, and structured health summaries could support astronaut health awareness when communication with Earth is limited.

ORBITAL is a demonstration prototype, not validated medical software.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

ORBITAL ("Know your signal.") is an offline-first health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions. A crew member logs 14 indicators: heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood glucose, temperature, SpO2, sleep duration, mood, stress, hydration, exercise, radiation dose, body mass, and energy intake. A separate wellbeing check-in records mood, sleep quality, isolation, crew conflict, workload, and an optional private note.

A rules engine classifies each reading as nominal, caution, or warning against configurable demonstration thresholds. Missing readings are labeled "No data" and never treated as normal. Readings are also compared with a rolling 7-day mean and the mean of prior logged readings.

Each alert explains what is happening, why it matters in spaceflight, and what to do next. It also shows the triggering rule, linked hazard, confidence label, and escalation label.

Other features:

- Interactive body map with 8 systems, each linked to its spaceflight hazard and recent readings.

- Trend charts for 7 days, 30 days, or the full mission, with a personal reference band, flagged readings, and a simple linear early-warning estimate (needs at least 3 readings in the last 14 days).

- Demonstration health score: starts at 100, minus 24 per red alert, minus 10 per yellow alert, plus up to 6 for recent records, bounded 0 to 100.

- Coach section for logging exercise and showing general hydration, nutrition, sleep, radiation-event, and wellbeing reminders.

- Ask Doc: offline, button-selected answers from a small rules base. It is not a conversational AI and directs urgent situations to crew and mission procedures.

- Handoff: a 7-day summary of alerts, readings, and actions for a flight surgeon, which can be copied or printed. The queue is local only.

- Five mission modes (ISS/LEO, Orion transit, lunar base, Mars transit, Mars surface) that change hazard emphasis and alert ordering.

- A 180-day synthetic Mars-transit simulator with a radiation spike (days 73-75), sleep disruption (days 92-99), exercise gap (days 120-131), glucose drift (from day 133), and mood dip (days 146-158), plus buttons to inject radiation, fever, missed-sleep, and glucose events.

BENEFITS

- Works with no connection, which matters when Earth cannot respond quickly (we modeled an illustrative 22-minute one-way delay for Mars modes).

- Alerts are explainable, so the crew can see why each one fired.

- Raw logs become a structured summary for ground medical staff.

- Nothing to install or configure: it opens from a single HTML file.

INTENDED IMPACT

To demonstrate that local, transparent, hazard-aware monitoring can support crew autonomy in deep space, and give ground medical teams a clear summary when contact is possible. We modeled five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile closed environments.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript.

- Graphics: inline SVG for charts, the body map, and the score gauge.

- Storage: browser localStorage (key "orbital-state") with an in-memory fallback.

- Delivery: one self-contained HTML file, hosted on GitHub. No framework, package manager, backend, API key, or network requests.

- Hardware: none beyond a computer or phone with a modern browser. No sensors or wearables are connected.

- Testing: a built-in self-test (window.orbitalSelfTest()) with four checks (nominal heart rate, temperature caution, low-SpO2 warning, low-mood wellbeing alert), plus manual checks that all ten views render and the simulator generates 180 records and responds to event injection.

- Reference material: public NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CSA resources, linked in the app. They do not validate our thresholds.

CREATIVITY

- Alerts are tied to spaceflight hazards and mission mode, not generic health ranges.

- The body map connects each body system to the hazard that threatens it.

- The 180-day simulator lets anyone see the full pipeline (reading, alert, trend, handoff) in minutes.

- The whole app is dependency-free and opens by double-clicking one file.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Offline operation: no connection required.

- Explainability: every alert exposes its rule and reasoning.

- Honest uncertainty: confidence labels, rough-estimate wording, no clinical claims.

- Privacy: no accounts and no data transmitted. Local storage is not encrypted, and the app states this.

- Accessibility: keyboard-operable controls, text labels alongside status colors, responsive layout for phones, and reduced-motion support.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

ORBITAL is not a medical device. Thresholds, score, forecasts, and simulated data are for demonstration only. It does not ingest wearable data, use a trained predictive model, encrypt records, or connect to any space agency system. Next steps: clinically validated thresholds, encrypted storage, wearable and sensor ingestion, secure crew-to-ground handoff sync, strict mission-start baselines, and expanded automated tests.

Repository: https://github.com/Afsal-Mhd-Ai/orbital-astronaut-health-monitoring.git
